A new chemical plant opened this week at BASF’s manufacturing complex in Geismar, Louisiana, completing a roughly $1 billion expansion that began in 2018. The project nearly doubles the site’s capacity for methylene diphenyl diisocyanate, or MDI, to about 600,000 metric tons a year.
What’s Related
BASF confirmed that the new plant has started up. The company called the expansion its largest wholly owned investment in North America and said the added capacity makes it the region’s largest MDI producer.
“With this expansion, BASF is taking the lead in MDI production in North America,” said Ramkumar Dhruva, president of BASF’s Monomers Division. The company did not say when it expects the site to reach its full annual capacity.
Three-phase expansion
BASF carried out the project in three phases at its existing Geismar complex in Ascension Parish. A new unit for making MDI began operating in October 2020. In 2021, BASF expanded several units that feed into MDI production, increasing the complex’s capacity by about a third.
BASF broke ground on the final phase in January 2023 after announcing a $780 million investment in that portion of the project. The final phase added units for earlier steps in the manufacturing process, along with equipment that separates the chemical into different products. BASF said the new equipment gives the plant more flexibility to adjust production to customer needs.
What is MDI?
Manufacturers use MDI to make polyurethane, a material found in building insulation and appliances. It’s also used in vehicles, furniture, and footwear. By expanding at Geismar, BASF can make more of the chemical closer to its North American customers while using the infrastructure and raw material supply already in place at the complex.
The project also expanded production capacity for aniline, a chemical used to make MDI. BASF said it can now sell aniline directly from Geismar to North American customers that make agricultural chemicals, rubber, dyes and pigments.

LTL carrier XPO is now an investment-grade credit at one of the three major ratings agencies.
Fitch Ratings has upgraded its rating on XPO (NYSE: XPO) to BBB-. That is one notch above the cutoff between investment-grade and non-investment grade debt.
It comes just a few months after both Moody’s (NYSE: MCO) and S&P Global Ratings (NYSE: SPGI) raised their ratings on XPO by one notch, BB+ at S&P Global and Ba1 at Moody’s. Both those grades are considered equivalent, but they are also both below the cutoff between investment grade and non investment grade debt.
Fitch first rated XPO in March 2023. Its first grade was BB+. It held that rating until the most recent change.
“The upgrade reflects robust operating and commercial execution and structural improvement in XPO’s business and cash flows at a pace above the industry,” Fitch said in its report released late last week. “Significant gross debt repayment shows swift, meaningful commitment to publicly stated leverage targets in 2026.”
As a publicly-traded company, XPO’s financial situation is well-known, unlike companies that are privately-held but which have publicly-traded debt.
Between the third quarters of 2025 and 2026, XPO saw its revenue rise 12.4% to $2.37 billion, saw net income climb to $181 million from $82 million, and improved its adjusted operating ratio to 80.1% from 82.7%.
But from the perspective of a ratings agency like Fitch, a more important number would be that in the nine months ending September 30, its repayment of debt climbed to more than $1 billion from $50 million in the corresponding period of 2025.
Cash flow also is king for ratings agencies, and Fitch liked what it sees at XPO.
“XPO’s financial flexibility benefits from stronger free cash flow (FCF), which Fitch forecasts at around $500 million in 2026 and 2027, on a Fitch-calculated basis, up from about $270 million in 2025,” the agency said. Fitch noted that it has a proprietary method for measuring cash flow.
Two key benchmarks–EBITDA and EBITDAR to debt, with the R in EBITDAR representing rent costs–will be in the low 2.0X range this year at XPO, Fitch said. That is down from 2.8X and 2.7X, respectively, from the 2025 figure. “The announced focus on internal initiatives over large inorganic growth and balanced debt and equity repurchase deployment in 2026, indicated a strategy to maintain leverage,” Fitch said.
Fitch made comparisons of XPO’s debt ratings to three other companies. One is Brink’s of armored car fame, but the only overlap is that they transport something, though what Brinks is hauling isn’t what one would find in the back of an LTL truck.
The two other comparisons were to TFI International (NYSE: TFII) and Forward Air. Fitch does not have a rating on TFI International. But it said TFI’s historical average debt load is in the mid 1.0X to low 2.0X range. Forward Air, on the other hand, is now forecast to have recorded a debt load of more than 6.0X in 2026, improving to mid-5.0X range in 2028.
Forward Air’s (NASDAQ: FWRD) rating at Fitch is B with a negative outlook. That is five notches less than the new rating for XPO at Fitch.
The outlook on XPO is stable, which means an upgrade or downgrade is not likely in the foreseeable future.
In recent years, the reports of ratings agencies about the state of trucking have been pessimistic, with LTL carriers getting just a slightly more optimistic outlook.
But the Fitch report was upbeat on the prospects for the LTL sector.
“Fitch expects the LTL industry’s profitability to be resilient through business cycles,” it said. “This reflects the competitive barriers tied to established asset-based networks. XPO and other large LTL operators have demonstrated a higher degree of pricing rationality through freight cycles relative to the truckload market. Contractual relationships in LTL also offer some additional cyclical stability over spot truckload markets, though typical contract tenors are one year.”
XPO’s stock is up about 36.7% in the last year. It’s up about 3% in the last month and down about 7% in the last three months.
XPO does not pay a dividend. In its notes about developments that could change its rating on XPO, Fitch mentioned “a deviation from capital allocation plans, such as initiating a large dividend or mergers and acquisitions (M&A) strategy that restricts financial flexibility.”
XPO’s last significant acquisition was for real estate being divested by the bankrupt Yellow Corp. in 2024.

With 10 active or planned Phase 3 trials underway for Metsera’s berobenatide, Pfizer has signed a deal with Blackstone Life Sciences to finance the program to approval.
Pfizer has secured up to $1.5 billion in private equity funding from Blackstone Life Sciences to support the Metsera-acquired obesity drug berobenatide as the New York pharma faces a tough loss of exclusivity period for several top products.
Blackstone will provide the funding for the GLP-1 receptor agonist berobenatide through 2028 in exchange for undisclosed regulatory and commercial milestones if the drug is approved in the U.S., according to a Wednesday evening press release . Pfizer will retain full ownership and decision-making power over the program as well as the broader commercial opportunity, BMO Capital Markets pointed out in a Wednesday note.
“We like the deal structure, particularly given where Pfizer sits in its upcoming LOE cycle,” BMO wrote. “Pfizer retains full operational control and ownership of berobenatide, meaning the agreement meaningfully offsets near-term development spending without giving away the asset or its topline sales opportunity.”
Leerink Partners said the money will be paid out over the term, with the amounts increasing over time.
Berobenatide is a long-acting injectable therapy for weight management. Pfizer has a massive—and expensive—clinical program for the investigational therapy, including 10 ongoing or planned Phase 3 trials in chronic weight management and obesity-related conditions such as knee osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnea. The drug was acquired via the $10 billion deal for Metsera last year, which Pfizer won in a bidding war with established weight loss magnate Novo.

BMO said the timing makes sense, as Pfizer is facing a crunch of LOEs across its portfolio. The deal “allows the company to preserve financial flexibility while continuing to invest behind what has emerged as a potentially important obesity franchise,” the firm wrote.
Leerink expects the deal to help Pfizer over the next two years as it heads toward a patent cliff for the blockbuster blood thinner Eliquis, which begins in April 2028.
But not all details were disclosed, with nothing declared on the potential milestones that Blackstone could be eligible for, which makes the true cost of the deal hard to calculate, BMO said: “Consequently, while the near-term benefit of shifting up to $1.5B of development expense externally is clear, we think it is difficult to quantify the ultimate impact on Pfizer’s longer-term cash generation if berobenatide becomes a successful commercial product.”
This is not the first major deal that Blackstone has done with a Big Pharma. The PE giant signed a similar agreement with Merck in 2025 to fund the development of the TROP2 antibody-drug conjugate sac-TMT. Blackstone offered $700 million to cover development costs for the asset through 2026 in exchange for royalties on net sales for all approved indications the drug achieves.
The deal comes a week after Pfizer announced new CFO Cecile Guegan during third quarter earnings. The pharma grew 7% operationally, with its COVID portfolio dragging on earnings. New and acquired products, however, saw 32% year-over-year growth. These include Padcev, an ADC from the 2023 Seagen acquisition and the migraine medicine Nurtec, picked up from Biohaven .
Guegan said during a Nov. 3 analyst call that Pfizer will continue to put its muscle behind these products to mitigate the LOEs to come.

Defense electronics are undergoing a rapid shift, as responding to emerging threats in real-time demands a faster process to deployment. (Photo illustration courtesy of Frontgrade.)
Military necessity to respond to emerging threats in near-real time is putting pressure on a traditional acquisition process built on lengthy Research, Development, Test, and Evaluation (RDT&E) cycles before a new capability can pass to warfighters. Nowhere is that more apparent than in radio frequency (RF) technology, where rapidly changing electronic warfare (EW) threats, new communications requirements for command and control, and expanding missions are forcing the defense industrial base to deliver more capability in less time.
The challenge extends beyond designing faster processors or more powerful RF amplifiers. Defense electronics must meet increasingly demanding size, weight, power, and thermal constraints for autonomous platforms, for example, while remaining adaptable to new waveforms, frequencies, and operational requirements. At the same time, supply-chain limitations and production schedules are the determining factor in how quickly those systems reach the warfighter.
For companies supplying electronics to prime contractors, the answer increasingly involves adapting proven designs rather than developing every capability from scratch. That approach reduces technical risk, shortens qualification timelines, and makes it easier to integrate new functionality into existing platforms.
“We don’t have time to field an entire platform, come back, see what happens, go do another one,” said Lorne Graves, senior vice president and chief technology officer at Frontgrade Technologies [Frontgrade]. “Those days are gone.”
Adapting to threats faster than traditional acquisition allows
As mentioned, there’s a mismatch between the pace of technological change and the time required to develop, qualify, and produce military electronics. For RF systems used in EW, tactical communications, radar, and space applications, requirements can change considerably during a traditional acquisition cycle. An architecture developed for one threat environment may need to accommodate different frequencies, waveforms, or operating conditions by the time it is fielded.
That puts a premium on adaptable hardware and designs that allow new capabilities to be introduced without replacing an entire subsystem.
“The time it takes to respond to these threats means that you wouldn’t field the platform,” said Graves. “The architecture better have adaptability to be able to change and counter those threats.”
Such adaptability doesn’t come from pursuing highly customized solutions for every requirement. Rather, the solution is increasingly the application of commercially developed capabilities and existing qualified designs “to effectively get a good enough solution without having to create a very bespoke solution to meet a very narrow set of requirements,” said Jack Kilian, senior vice president and chief growth officer for Frontgrade.
In practice, that could mean beginning with a design that already meets 80 percent of a program’s requirements, then adapting particular functions, interfaces, or performance characteristics. It could also involve qualification by “similarity”, using evidence from an existing design to reduce the testing needed for a related configuration, according to Kilian.
For the military, the advantage is not simply a shorter procurement timeline as it facilitates the bringing of evolved capabilities to the field sooner while preserving a path for subsequent upgrades as the threat changes.
Adapting proven designs to meet needs speeds up the delivery timeline for new technologies. (Photo illustration courtesy of Frontgrade.)
Supply chain resilience becomes part of the mission
The same emphasis on speed is changing how electronics suppliers manage manufacturing capacity. RF systems depend on specialized semiconductors, materials, and mechanical components that can be difficult to source. Gallium nitride, widely used in high-performance RF applications, illustrates the challenge because of supply-chain exposure involving the raw gallium required for its production.
Kilian noted the concentration of gallium production in China and the export restrictions that have increased concerns about access to critical materials. Bearings, magnets, and other components can also create lengthy production delays.
Frontgrade is addressing those risks through multiple sourcing, strategic inventories of critical parts, and greater internal manufacturing capability. The company is qualifying additional suppliers to reduce dependence on individual manufacturers, and maintaining stocks of components used across multiple product lines so production teams can respond more quickly without committing inventory to a single, specialized design. Standardizing certain components across products can substantially shorten delivery schedules.
“It can significantly pull in these lead times from beyond 52 weeks to below 26 weeks in many cases for these deliverables,” said Kilian. That means, for example, that Frontgrade can get critical hardware and electronics into a prime contractor’s hands for integration onto a communications satellite.
Integrating the electronics backbone
Frontgrade’s advanced RF capabilities have expanded through the addition of Aethercomm (acquired in 2023), IDSI (the Defense Solutions division of Crescend Technologies acquired in 2025), and Tricom Research (2025), complementing its existing portfolio of antennas, radiation-hardened electronics, processing, and power technologies.
Together, those capabilities cover a substantial portion of the signal chain from RF signal acquisition and conditioning through conversion, digital processing, and storage – whether they be individual components or larger integrated systems.
“Our prime customers are looking for partners that can effectively deliver integrated subsystem solutions that are ready to layer their application software on top of it,” said Kilian, noting in that arrangement that suppliers like Frontgrade can deliver hardware together with the middleware and application programming interfaces needed to support higher-level software integration.
Customers can purchase components to build their own boards, obtain board-level subsystems, or use more complete integrated systems that already combine RF, digital conversion, processing, and storage. The objective is to let prime contractors concentrate on the application and mission requirements rather than having to integrate every underlying electronic component themselves.
For military users, the implications extend across multiple mission areas. EW, radar, SATCOM, and counter-UAS systems operate across different frequency bands, but they share the need for efficient RF amplification, signal conditioning, and reliable performance under demanding environmental conditions.
The company’s acquired RF capabilities from the acquisitions mentioned above include technologies with a storied history in counter-improvised explosive device (IED) systems dating to the early 2000s – particularly the Counter Radio-Controlled Improvised Explosive Device Electronic Warfare (CREW) system that jammed RF signals that set off IEDs. That heritage also informs applications involving counter-UAS and other EW missions.
Another important requirement for today’s military electronics is delivering greater RF power from smaller packages while controlling thermal loads. Frontgrade provides efficient power amplifiers for small spaces that operate in high-thermal environments. Those attributes’ constraints are especially significant in space, where spacecraft cannot rely on the cooling approaches commonly available in terrestrial data centers and communications facilities.
The result is an engineering tradeoff in which power output, efficiency, packaging, and thermal performance is considered together rather than optimized independently.
Building adaptability into the hardware
The next step is making RF electronics easier to modify after the initial system design has been completed. Graves distinguishes between scalability, which generally involves expanding an existing capability, and extensibility, which allows proven technology to be adapted for different operating environments and mission requirements.
Common design elements developed for space, counter-UAS, and EW applications can serve as starting points for related systems. Using previously qualified modules can reduce development effort and enable suppliers to meet more demanding deployment schedules.
For example, that philosophy informs the design of Frontgrade’s power amplifiers. Rather than treating an amplifier as fixed hardware with a single operating configuration, Frontgrade is incorporating telemetry, health monitoring, and software-controlled features that allow performance to be adjusted to changing requirements. Those features support changes in power efficiency and waveform characteristics without necessarily requiring a hardware replacement.
Graves described these devices as “smart” power amplifiers, with controls intended to make the RF chain more responsive to operational requirements. The distinction becomes critical for equipment deployed in space as physical access to satellites is generally unavailable, making software adaptability considerably more important.
With having software-controlled RF capabilities, operators can adapt to interference and maintain communications links needed to deliver information to warfighters. The goal is to preserve the usefulness of existing hardware as threats and mission requirements evolve rather than treating every new requirement as a reason to redesign the system.

Seven H.B. Fuller manufacturing sites in North America and Europe will shut down as the adhesives maker moves production into fewer plants. The company announced the closures earlier this week and said some work is moving to a new aerospace manufacturing site in Charlotte, North Carolina, and to a plant that recently began operating in Monterrey, Mexico .
What’s Related
The closures are part of a plan H.B. Fuller outlined in 2025 to consolidate manufacturing and distribution. The company had 64 manufacturing sites worldwide at the end of its fiscal third quarter, down from 82 at the end of 2024. It expects to be down to 55 by 2030.
“We have moved decisively from planning to execution, and these results validate the opportunity to increase efficiency, reduce operating costs, and better serve our customers,” said Celeste Mastin, H.B. Fuller’s president and CEO. The company did not name the seven sites, give individual closure dates, or say how many jobs would be affected.
Where the work is going
H.B. Fuller said in May that it expected the Charlotte facility to open in early 2027. The plant will bring aerospace adhesive production, packaging , testing and quality checks under one roof. It will have specialized mixing equipment and labs for developing and testing products.
The Monterrey plant is already running. H.B. Fuller did not specify which product lines would move to each location or when the transfers would be complete. The company expects operating costs for production moved to newer facilities to fall by as much as 50%.
Plans for North America
H.B. Fuller is also reorganizing North American distribution around six regional centers. It expects those centers to handle about 60% of its North American volume by 2030 and says the change will put products closer to customers.
The company expects the number of locations it ships from via less-than-truckload carriers to fall by more than 80%. That means carriers would pick up those shipments from far fewer locations. H.B. Fuller also expects the change to give it more control over inventory and reduce the amount of cash tied up in stock.
$75 million in annual savings
H.B. Fuller expects the manufacturing and distribution plan to save $75 million annually by 2030. It expects to reach about $25 million in annualized savings by the end of fiscal 2026 and add another $20 million to $25 million in savings in 2027.
The company expects capital spending on the project to fall below $25 million in 2027, after about $100 million in total investment through 2026. It expects spending to decline further after 2027 as more production moves to newer plants that require less investment in maintenance.
